newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: CA executives hold breath as sale deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: CA executives hold breath as sale deadline looms.

text.p: Executives at Austrian selloff candidate Creditanstalt were holding their breath on Thursday, hours before a final deadline for bids in Europe's longest running privatisation project was scheduled to close.

The battle for control of the country's second biggest bank has put the bank's management on the defensive and deeply divided a fragile government coalition of the dominant Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima has given bidders a final breathing space until 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Friday to adjust existing offers for the state's controlling stake in the bank. He is expected to announce the winning bid over the weekend.

Bank Austria, tipped as the future owner of Creditanstalt, declined to say whether a special meeting of its supervisory board late on Thursday had voted to polish up what is widely regarded as the leading offer.

But sources close to the talks said that would hardly be necessary since the bank's 16.8 million schilling bid for the state's 70 percent voting stake in its main competitor already exceeds a rival offer by EA-Generali and its partners.

The consortium, which includes Italian and German interests and is backed by the conservatives, said on Wednesday it had topped up its previous offer of 13.8 billion schillings for the bank stake, but declined to say by how much.

Creditanstalt chief executive Guido Schmidt-Chiari, in what may have been his last news conference before he has to clear out his desk, failed to impress observers on Thursday when he presented a 20 percent rise in the bank's 1996 net profit.
Analysts said the figures were papering over what in reality was a comparatively weak performance, and investors knocked Creditanstalt's shares down one percent on the Vienna bourse.

"It looks like they're squeezing all that they can out to paint a pretty picture (ahead of the sale)," said James Capel analyst Claire Fargeot, adding that the figures looked better at face value than they were fundamentally.

Schmidt-Chiari, appealing for a last-minute rethink in what appears to be all but a done deal, warned the shares may fall further if Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled and backed by the Social-Democratic dominated City of Vienna, would get its hands on Austria's establishment bank.

But his main ally in the battle to keep Creditanstalt firmly in the conservative camp, the People's Party, appeared at least in principle ready to let go of its stronghold -- if only at a potentially high price for Bank Austria.

In a statement, the party said it was confident of finding a parliamentary majority for its proposal that would force Bank Austria to pay the same price to small shareholders which it has offered for the state's stake. That move alone could cost the bank an extra 7.2 billion schillings.
The People's Party has already held talks with the far-right opposition. A vote against the Social Democrats could put the survival of the fractious government in danger.

The conservatives have called for a special parliamentary session on the sale on Tuesday. Coalition leaders agreed to hold an emergency meeting on Saturday to try and iron out their differences, but Klima left little doubt he would ignore conservative warnings not to make a decision before Tuesday.

"The Bank Austria offer is the highest and strategically the best," he said. "And if I don't sell to the highest bidder I automatically break European Union law -- and every Austrian would also have the right to sue me."
